To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combination of modulation-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC) with convolutional neural networks (CNN) is the best performing system in terms of classification accuracy, but requires more than 100x the computing resources compared to MFCC with recurrent neural networks (RNN).
the performance of the proposed system can reach a classification accuracy of 0.95 for the considered acoustic events.

the combination of MFCC features and DNN classification achieves state-of-the-art results for acoustic event detection in realistic multisource conditions and that the use of a DNN classifier is a viable alternative to the traditional GMM-HMM based approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how to best use the limited computing resources on distributed devices while maintaining a good classification accuracy.
two issues: Firstly, the classification performance of acoustic event detectors in realistic, however, challenging conditions.
the evaluation of the performance of different classifiers in the context of a distributed system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while deep learning approaches are indeed very powerful and achieve state-of-the-art results, they are not necessarily the best solution for every use case.
the use of modulation features, especially in conjunction with MFCCs, is beneficial for acoustic event classification in general.
the performance of the best DNN classifier is superior to all other methods, but at a cost.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the performance of traditional techniques is not competitive in the current state-of-the-art, however the computational resources required to achieve this level of performance are not prohibitive for embedded systems.

the classification accuracy of deep learning models is significantly higher than that of traditional techniques, but at the cost of a higher computational load, especially when the feature dimensionality is high.
deep learning based classification is able to outperform the baseline system, but that a large amount of training data is necessary.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a combination of modulation-frequency cepstral coefficients (Modulation-MFCC) and deep convolutional networks is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance in a distributed scenario, while at the same time being able to run on low-power embedded devices.

a simple, yet efficient, convolutional model, i.e. a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) can outperform more complex models in terms of classification accuracy while requiring less than 1/10 of the computing resources.

, even in the absence of large-scale training data, a simple convolutional neural network architecture is able to achieve a performance that is competitive with state-of-the-art deep-learning-based approaches.
